identity.title: MotionStream: Real-Time Video Generation with Interactive Motion Controls

problem.claim: Real-time, interactively controlled video generation is hindered by minute-scale latency and non-causal processing.

gap.claim: Existing motion-conditioned methods do not support on-the-fly real-time interaction because of these latency and causality limitations.

contributions.claim: MotionStream distills a bidirectional motion-controlled text-to-video teacher into a causal student using Self Forcing with Distribution Matching Distillation.
It combines sliding-window causal attention, attention sinks, self-rollout, and KV-cache rolling to support fixed-context streaming over arbitrarily long videos.
It provides interactive controls including painted trajectories, camera control, and motion transfer during streaming generation.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish MotionStream as enabling infinite-length streaming with constant-speed generation and interactive motion controls.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report sub-second latency and up to 29 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU.
The authors report state-of-the-art motion following and video quality, alongside a two-orders-of-magnitude speed improvement.
The authors report real-time unfolding of results for trajectory painting, camera control, and motion transfer.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper identifies latency and non-causality as barriers to interactive motion-conditioned video generation.
A motion-augmented text-to-video model follows global text and local motion guidance but remains unsuitable for on-the-fly inference.
The bidirectional teacher is distilled into a causal student for streaming inference.
Sliding-window attention, attention sinks, self-rollout, and KV-cache rolling address extrapolation, error accumulation, and fixed-cost inference.
The authors report fast, high-quality motion following with interactive controls and infinite-length streaming.

source_observation.claim: The abstract explicitly separates finite-horizon training from infinite-horizon deployment and names extrapolation, error accumulation, and context-cost growth as distinct challenges.

lessons.interpretation: A strong technical narrative can map each deployment constraint to a named design response.
lessons.application: When presenting a long-horizon generation method, enumerate deployment failure modes and link each to a specific mechanism or training procedure.
lessons.exception: This structure is less suitable when the system has no meaningful horizon, latency, or accumulation constraints.

unknowns: The abstract gives no benchmark names, metric values, baselines, or experimental conditions supporting the state-of-the-art and speed comparisons.
The meaning and operational evaluation of “infinite-length” streaming are unspecified.
The abstract does not quantify interaction latency or assess control quality separately for trajectories, cameras, and motion transfer.
